readme.summary: Audited README.md (372 lines) at v1.0-fixes HEAD (71d863a) against code, benchmark JSONs, docs, and live links. The good news: nearly all performance claims are traceable and accurate — the 257-354x BLS-vs-astropy range matches benchmarks/results/by_gpu/*.json exactly (256.9x A100 to 353.7x L40 across exactly 7 GPUs), the BLS survey table (802/38/236/6 LC/s; $0.69/$14.74/$1.22/$2.00), LS-vs-nifty-ls table (4.4/19.2/3.3/19.8 ms/LC; >27x/>15x/1.5x/12.6x; N_freq 365K/1.825M/13.5K/730K), $33 total ($32.96 in docs/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md), Keplerian 4-37x, and $0.14/M on RTX 4000 Ada all match docs/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md and the JSONs. API claims verified against code: eebls_gpu returns (power, solutions) and eebls_gpu_fast_adaptive returns power only, so the Quick Start compiles against current signatures (float64 y is cast internally); eebls_transit defaults (use_gpu=True, sparse_threshold=500), sparse_bls_gpu/cpu, PDM's 8 kinds + (t,y,err) API, CE compute_log_prob/normalization/overflow-guard/use_fast+weighted ValueError, TLS import UserWarning + ~3,500-point ValueError, Python>=3.9, numpy>=1.17/scipy>=1.3, CUDA 11.8 Dockerfile, CI matrix 3.9-3.12 + wheel smoke test, and PR #57-#62 merges all check out. All linked repo files exist and all external URLs resolve. The release-blocking problems are distribution/doc-channel mismatches: PyPI's latest release is 0.2.5, so the badge, 'pip install cuvarbase' instructions, and Quick Start are mutually contradictory (the PyPI version has none of the v1.0 API); the three links to https://johnh2o2.github.io/cuvarbase/ point to a gh-pages site last built in 2017 that documents the v0.2.x API (and is cited as the 'new documentation' for PDM); the claimed periodograms/ module does not exist; and examples/ does not contain the LS/CE examples the README promises (those live in unreferenced notebooks/). On the selling point: the headline pitch ('GPU-accelerated time series analysis tools for astronomy') is one line and is well supported, but the strongest evidence (TESS QLP production use since Sector 59, 257-354x, all-surveys-for-$33) is buried at lines 56-64 below ~50 lines of citation BibTeX and personal history — reordering existing sections (no restyling) would put the supported pitch in the first screenful.

confirmed.title: PyPI install instructions and badge point to v0.2.5, which has none of the documented v1.0 API
confirmed.detail: README lines 239-243 say 'Install from PyPI: pip install cuvarbase' and line 3 carries the badge.fury.io PyPI badge. Live PyPI query (June 12, 2026) returns latest version 0.2.5 (releases 0.2.1-0.2.5; note CHANGELOG.rst line 4 says the last PyPI release was 0.2.6, which also contradicts PyPI — the v0.2.6 git tag exists but was never published). A user who follows the README's primary install path gets 2017-era code with no eebls_gpu_fast_adaptive, no sparse_bls_gpu/cpu, no PDM variants, no Python-3-only packaging — so the Quick Start (line 288, bls.eebls_gpu_fast_adaptive) fails with AttributeError, and every 'What's New in v1.0' feature is absent. The badge will also render 'pypi v0.2.5' directly above a README describing v1.0.

Also reconcile CHANGELOG's '0.2.6' claim with PyPI's actual 0.2.5.

confirmed.title: Adaptive-BLS 'parity to ~1.3x' claim understates the floor in its own cited benchmark (0.48x at ndata=50)
confirmed.detail: Lines 102-110 say the adaptive kernel 'measures parity to ~1.3x over the fixed-block kernel on realistic Keplerian grids', citing benchmarks/results/bls_adaptive_keplerian_benchmark_rtxa5000_jun2026.json. That JSON's speedup_vs_std spans 0.481x (ndata=50, nfreq=306214 — adaptive 2x slower, albeit with a large std_time of 0.0118 suggesting noise) and 0.916x (ndata=64) up to 1.330x (ndata=200). So the measured range is 0.48-1.33x, not 'parity to 1.3x'. CHANGELOG.rst phrases it as '~1.0-1.3x', which also glosses the sub-parity points.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Say 'roughly parity (0.9-1.3x, with one noisy 0.5x outlier at ndata=50) over the fixed-block kernel' or re-run the ndata=50 point to resolve whether the 0.48x is real before keeping the parity claim.

rst-docs.summary: Audited all 9 Sphinx doc sources in /Users/johnhoffman/Documents/cuvarbase/docs/source/ at v1.0-fixes HEAD (71d863a) against the current cuvarbase API. Overall: pdm.rst is current and accurate; the appended "Power-spectrum convention" and "Unsupported option combinations" sections in bls/lomb/ce.rst are accurate against the code; but the build configuration and several examples are stale. (1) A Sphinx build fails IMMEDIATELY on any modern machine because conf.py:85 loads 'matplotlib.sphinxext.only_directives', which was removed in matplotlib 3.0 (verified absent in local matplotlib 3.9.4) — this is independent of GPU availability. (2) conf.py has NO autodoc_mock_imports / sys.modules mocking; cuvarbase/__init__.py:2 does 'import pycuda.autoprimaryctx' at top level, so on a GPU-less machine every automodule directive in cuvarbase.rst and cuvarbase.tests.rst fails at import (autodoc downgrades these to warnings, and docs/Makefile has no -W, so the build would "complete" with empty API pages — but only after the extension blocker is fixed). To rebuild with the SAME theme/layout: theme is alabaster (bundled with Sphinx) + html_logo=logo.png + custom html_sidebars (about/navigation/relations/searchbox/donate) — all reproducible with stock 'pip install sphinx matplotlib numpy scipy' PLUS two conf.py changes: drop the only_directives extension and add autodoc_mock_imports=['pycuda','skcuda'] (cufinufft/batman are already try/except-guarded in the package; pytest is additionally needed if keeping the cuvarbase.tests autodoc page). Caveat: the 4 GPU-executing plot_directive figures (bls_example, bls_example_transit, bls_transit_diagram, ce_example) cannot render without a real GPU AND currently crash on numpy>=1.20/1.24 anyway (np.int/np.float/float linspace num) — plot_directive failures are warnings, so pages build with :include-source: code but missing images; figures need a GPU build (or committed images) after fixing the numpy idioms. (3) API check of examples: lomb.rst and pdm.rst examples match current signatures; ce.rst example has a NameError (bare ConditionalEntropyAsyncProcess after 'import cuvarbase.ce as ce'); bls_example_transit.py passes nonexistent kwargs fmin_fac/fmax_fac (real names: fmin_frac/fmax_frac — silently swallowed by **kwargs); lomb.rst's leading 'import skcuda.fft' breaks the numpy>=1.24 shim ordering. bls.rst's sparse-BLS section matches eebls_transit/sparse_bls_cpu exactly (threshold 500, use_sparse, return tuple). (4) install.rst includes INSTALL.rst, which is the stalest page: CUDA 8.0, conda python=2.7, Python-2 print statement, pycuda-2017.1.1 pin with dead pypi.python.org URL, obsolete macOS-CUDA section, and 'pip install cuvarbase' (which would install 0.2.6 since 1.0.0 is not on PyPI) — all contradicting the v1.0.0 Python>=3.9 requirement. (5) whatsnew.rst is a one-line '.. include:: ../../CHANGELOG.rst', so it is consistent with CHANGELOG.rst by construction; the only wrinkle is CHANGELOG referencing a 0.2.6 release that has no entry. No files were modified.

confirmed.title: No autodoc mocking of pycuda/skcuda — all automodule pages fail at import on a GPU-less machine
confirmed.detail: conf.py has no autodoc_mock_imports and no sys.modules MagicMock setup (verified: zero matches for mock in conf.py). cuvarbase/__init__.py:2 executes 'import pycuda.autoprimaryctx' at package import (creates a CUDA context — requires driver+GPU even if pycuda is installed), and bls.py:14-17, ce.py:16-20, pdm.py:6-8, lombscargle.py:11-20 (also 'import skcuda.fft'), cunfft.py, tls.py:30-33 all import pycuda at module top level. Every automodule in cuvarbase.rst (bls, bls_frequencies, ce, core, cufinufft_backend, cunfft, lombscargle, pdm, tls*, utils, memory.*, base.async_process) and cuvarbase.tests.rst therefore fails to import. autodoc converts these to warnings and the Makefile (SPHINXOPTS = -E -a, no -W) won't abort, so the HTML would build with EMPTY API pages — i.e. the build 'succeeds' mechanically but the modules.rst/cuvarbase.rst content is lost. The root conftest.py pycuda/skcuda stubs only apply to pytest, not Sphinx.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Add autodoc_mock_imports = ['pycuda', 'skcuda'] to conf.py (cufinufft and batman are already guarded by try/except in cufinufft_backend.py and tls_models.py). scipy must be a real install (lombscargle.py and tls_stats.py import scipy.special/scipy.stats); add scipy (and pytest, if keeping the cuvarbase.tests autodoc page) to docs/requirements.txt.

confirmed.title: Rebuild recipe for same theme/layout (requested determination)
confirmed.detail: Theme is alabaster (conf.py:138) with html_logo='./logo.png' (file exists at docs/source/logo.png) and custom html_sidebars about/navigation/relations/searchbox/donate (conf.py:157-165) — alabaster ships as a Sphinx dependency, so the identical look is reproducible with stock Sphinx once the two conf.py issues above are fixed. Build entry: docs/Makefile ('python -msphinx', SPHINXOPTS='-E -a', not warning-fatal). Remaining caveats: (a) the 4 GPU plot_directive figures (bls.rst:13,20,73; ce.rst:15) execute real cuvarbase GPU code in-process — autodoc mocks do NOT apply to plot_directive, so on a GPU-less machine those figures emit warnings and render as source-only; generating images requires a GPU host (e.g. the RunPod flow) or committing prebuilt images, after fixing the numpy-2 idioms in the scripts; (b) docs/requirements.txt (sphinx, astropy, astrobase, numpy, matplotlib) is missing scipy and pytest, and 'astrobase' appears vestigial (referenced by nothing in docs/source/*.rst); (c) the two lomb.rst inline plots likewise need real pycuda/skcuda to produce figures and will warn-and-skip without a GPU.
confirmed.suggested_fix: pip install sphinx matplotlib numpy scipy pytest; edit conf.py per the two blocker findings; build with 'make html' in docs/; build on a GPU pod (scripts/runpod-*.sh) if the figures must be regenerated.

confirmed.title: ce.rst example raises NameError: ConditionalEntropyAsyncProcess used without ce. prefix
confirmed.detail: The example imports 'import cuvarbase.ce as ce' (ce.rst:23) but then calls 'proc = ConditionalEntropyAsyncProcess(phase_bins=10, mag_bins=5)' (ce.rst:33) with the bare class name, which is undefined — copy-pasting the example fails with NameError before any GPU work. confirmed.title: bls_example_transit.py passes nonexistent kwargs fmin_fac/fmax_fac to eebls_transit_gpu (silently ignored)
confirmed.detail: The :include-source: example for the Keplerian section passes 'fmin_fac=1.0, fmax_fac=1.5' in search_params (plots/bls_example_transit.py:95-96), but the actual parameters of eebls_transit_gpu are 'fmin_frac'/'fmax_frac' (bls.py:2151-2155). Because eebls_transit_gpu, fmin_transit, fmax_transit, transit_autofreq and eebls_gpu all take **kwargs catch-alls, the typo'd kwargs are SILENTLY swallowed — the example runs but the advertised fmax scaling of 1.5x never happens, and readers learn wrong parameter names. The other kwargs in the example (qmin_fac, qmax_fac, rho, samples_per_peak, dlogq, noverlap) and the 3-tuple return 'freqs, bls_power, sols' are correct for the current signature. The plain-BLS example (plots/bls_example.py) matches eebls_gpu(t, y, dy, freqs, qmin, qmax, dlogq, noverlap) at bls.py:1194 correctly.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Rename to fmin_frac=1.0, fmax_frac=1.5 in the example.

confirmed.title: lomb.rst examples start with 'import skcuda.fft' — unnecessary and breaks on numpy>=1.24
confirmed.detail: Both code examples (lomb.rst:102 and lomb.rst:144) begin with 'import skcuda.fft' before importing cuvarbase. cuvarbase.lombscargle applies the numpy compatibility shim (_skcuda_compat.ensure_numpy_aliases, lombscargle.py:16) BEFORE importing skcuda.fft (lombscargle.py:20); importing skcuda.fft directly as the first statement bypasses the shim, so with numpy>=1.24 (np.float removed) the example's very first line raises AttributeError inside the abandoned scikit-cuda 0.5.3. The import is also redundant — cuvarbase.lombscargle imports cufft itself. The rest of both examples is API-correct: LombScargleAsyncProcess(), proc.run([(t, y, dy)]) returning [(freqs, power)] (lombscargle.py:685-777), batched_run_const_nfreq(data) (lombscargle.py:778), proc.finish().

confirmed.title: (4) VERBATIM 2017 Keplerian-assumption text from origin/gh-pages:_sources/bls.rst.txt
confirmed.detail:
Section 'A shortcut: assuming orbital mechanics' (verbatim, including the literal TeX):

"If you assume :math:`R_p\ll R_{\star}`, :math:`M_p\ll M_{\star}`, :math:`L_p\ll L_{\star}`, and :math:`e\ll 1`,  where :math:`e` is the ellipticity of the planetary orbit, :math:`L` is the luminosity, :math:`R` is the radius, and :math:`M` mass, you can eliminate a free parameter.

This is because the orbital period obeys `Kepler's third law <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler's_laws_of_planetary_motion#Third_law>`_,

.. math::
	P^2 \approx \frac{4\pi^2a^3}{G(M_p + M_{\star})}

.. plot:: plots/planet_transit_diagram.py

The angle of the transit is

.. math::

	\theta = 2{\rm arcsin}\left(\frac{R_p + R_{\star}}{a}\right)

and :math:`q` is therefore :math:`\theta / (2\pi)`. Thus we have a relation between :math:`q` and the period :math:`P`

.. math::

	\sin{\pi q} = (R_p + R_{\star})\left(\frac{4\pi^2}{P^2 G(M_p + M_{\star})}\right)^{1/3}

By incorporating the fact that

.. math::
	
	R_{\star} = \left(\frac{3}{4\pi\rho_{\star}}\right)^{1/3}M_{\star}^{1/3}

where :math:`\rho_{\star}` is the average stellar density of the host star, we can write

.. math::

	\sin{\pi q} = \frac{(1 + r)}{(1 + m)^{1/3}} \left(\frac{3\pi}{G\rho_{\star}}\right)^{1/3} P^{-2/3}

where :math:`r = R_p / R_{\star}` and :math:`m = M_p / M_{\star}`. We can get rid of the constant factors and convert this to more intuitive units to obtain

.. math::

	\sin{\pi q} \approx 0.238 (1 + r - \frac{m}{3} + \dots{}) \left(\frac{\rho_{\star}}{\rho_{\odot}}\right)^{-1/3} \left(\frac{P}{\rm day}\right)^{-2/3}

where here we've expanded :math:`(1 + r) / (1 + m)^{1/3}` to first order in :math:`r` and :math:`m`."

This is followed by section 'Using the Keplerian assumption in ``cuvarbase``' whose entire body is:

".. plot:: plots/bls_example_transit.py
	:include-source:"

and by 'Period spacing considerations' (verbatim, relevant Keplerian paragraphs):

"The frequency spacing :math:`\delta f` needed to resolve a BLS signal with width :math:`q`, is

.. math::
	\delta f \lesssim \frac{q}{T}

where :math:`T` is the baseline of the observations (:math:`T = {\rm max}(t) - {\rm min}(t)`). This can be especially problematic if no assumptions are made about the nature of the signal (e.g., a Keplerian assumption). If you want to resolve a transit signal with a few observations, the minimum :math:`q` value that you would need to search is :math:`\propto 1/N` where :math:`N` is the number of observations.

For a typical Lomb-Scargle periodogram, the frequency spacing is :math:`\delta f \lesssim 1/T`, so running a BLS spectrum with an adequate frequency spacing over the same frequency range requires a factor of :math:`\mathcal{O}(N)` more trial frequencies, each of which requiring :math:`\mathcal{O}(N)` computations to estimate the best fit BLS parameters. That means that BLS scales as :math:`\mathcal{O}(N^2N_f)` while Lomb-Scargle only scales as :math:`\mathcal{O}(N_f\log N_f)`

However, if you can use the assumption that the transit is caused by an edge-on transit of a circularly orbiting planet, we not only eliminate a degree of freedom, but (assuming :math:`\sin{\pi q}\approx \pi q`)

.. math::
	
	\delta f \propto q \propto f^{2/3}

The minimum frequency you could hope to measure a transit period would be :math:`f_{\rm min} \approx 2/T`, and the maximum frequency is determined by :math:`\sin{\pi q} < 1` which implies

.. math::

	f_{max} = 8.612~{\rm c/day}~\times \left(1 - \frac{3r}{2} + \frac{m}{2} -\dots{}\right) \sqrt{\frac{\rho_{\star}}{\rho_{\odot}}}

For a 10 year baseline, this translates to :math:`2.7\times 10^5` trial frequencies. The number of trial frequencies needed to perform Lomb-Scargle over this frequency range is only about :math:`3.1\times 10^4`, so 8-10 times less. However, if we were to search the *entire* range of possible :math:`q` values at each trial frequency instead of making a Keplerian assumption, we would instead require :math:`5.35\times 10^8` trial frequencies, so the Keplerian assumption reduces the number of frequencies by over 1,000."

Note: this 2017 text survives verbatim as the first ~105 lines of today's docs/source/bls.rst (the O(N^2 N_f) scaling claim it contains is the one project memory flags as wrong — standard BLS is O(N x Nf)). The rendered bls.html section anchors are #a-shortcut-assuming-orbital-mechanics and #using-the-keplerian-assumption-in-cuvarbase.

keplerian-citation.summary: Citation research for cuvarbase's Keplerian transit-duration math is conclusive. The two papers to cite are (1) Ofir (2014) for the optimal frequency-grid spacing df = q(f)/(S*OS) with q ∝ f^(2/3), and (2) Seager & Mallén-Ornelas (2003) for the arcsin transit-duration equation underlying q_transit. I verified both papers' actual equations against the code: Ofir (2014) eq. (4) is Δf = q(f_true,M,R)/(S·OS) — exactly cuvarbase's `df = qmin_fac * q_transit(f)/(samples_per_peak * T)` in bls.py:282 and `df = q/(oversampling * T)` in bls_frequencies.py:91; Ofir eq. (2) is q(f,M,R) ≈ (2π)^(2/3)/π · R/(GM)^(1/3) · f^(2/3) (the small-angle form of cuvarbase's exact arcsin expression); Ofir Sect. 3.1 gives f_min = 2/S, matching `fmin2 = 2/(max(t)-min(t))` in bls.py:207; and Ofir eqs. (5)-(7) (A, C, N_freq for the cubic grid) are implemented verbatim in tls_grids.py:164-185. From the SMO03 PDF I confirmed eq. (3): t_T = (P/π)·arcsin{(R*/a)·[((1+Rp/R*)² − (a/R* · cos i)²)/(1 − cos²i)]^(1/2)} — with i = 90°, b = 0 this is exactly cuvarbase's q = t_T/P = arcsin((R*+Rp)/a)/π = arcsin((f/fmax0)^(2/3))/π in bls.py:215-220 and bls_frequencies.py:11-32; SMO03 eq. (4) is Kepler's third law P² = 4π²a³/(G(M*+Mp)) used in docs/source/bls.rst:32; SMO03 eq. (9) is the ρ*-from-transit-observables relation that justifies parameterizing q by stellar density ρ. benchmark-recon.summary: Reconnaissance complete for a master-vs-v1.0 / SOTA benchmark campaign on cuvarbase. origin/master (060d839, 2025-10-28, __version__=0.3.0, setup.py-only) has the same eebls_gpu_fast/eebls_gpu/eebls_transit_gpu signatures and qmin/qmax/dlogq/noverlap defaults as v1.0-fixes, but NO kernel caching (recompiles ~150ms+ per call unless functions= is passed), NO optimized/adaptive kernels, NO batch/sparse BLS, NO bls_frequencies.keplerian_freq_grid, and NO float64 epoch subtraction (raw float32 cast of t — BJD-scale timestamps silently destroy the phase fold; documented 0.961->0.002 power collapse). A true master comparison requires a separate venv/process (same package name + module-level pycuda.autoprimaryctx import); the existing in-repo "v0.4 baseline" (bench_bls_standard_gpu_old) is NOT master — at HEAD it now uses the kernel cache, so the published 21-390x "vs pre-v1.0" numbers are not reproducible from the current tree and conflate compilation-overhead removal with kernel gains. Benchmark infrastructure: scripts/benchmark_algorithms.py (cross-algorithm GPU-vs-CPU, CUDA-event timing, 1 warmup + 3 iters median, uniform non-survey freq grid, mismatched astropy duration grid), scripts/benchmark_new_features.py (SURVEY_PROFILES for ZTF/HAT-Net/TESS/Kepler, synchronized wall-clock timing), benchmark_adaptive_bls.py, benchmark_standard_bls.py, benchmark_all_gpus.sh (RunPod 7-GPU sweep driver). Prior claims live in docs/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md (BLS 257-354x vs astropy 7.2.0 across 7 GPUs; Keplerian grid 4.4-37.2x; LS vs nifty-ls 1.5-12.6x measured + timeout lower bounds; cuFINUFFT 0.63-0.84x; batch BLS 0.08x TESS regression) with raw JSON in benchmarks/results/{benchmark_results_new_features.json, by_gpu/*.json, bls_adaptive_keplerian_benchmark_rtxa5000_jun2026.json}. SOTA targets: astropy BoxLeastSquares (absolute-time duration arrays evaluated at every period, objective='likelihood'|'snr', method='fast', autoperiod(frequency_factor) grid — semantics differ from cuvarbase's fractional per-frequency q in [qmin,qmax] with dlogq/noverlap, so match work explicitly and compare timing+peak recovery, not power values); transitleastsquares (pip, multiprocessing use_threads, self-generated Ofir-2014 period grid you cannot inject — compare wall-time per LC at matched period range only; different statistic/model); fBLS (Shahaf 2022) has only a research-grade Jupyter-notebook repo github.com/saharsh1/fBLS (2 stars, last push Sep 2023, CPU-only) and is NOT on PyPI — no maintained fast public implementation; cuvarbase's own GPU-FFA experiment lost ~14x to adaptive+Keplerian (docs/FBLS_GPU_SPEC.md, archived). Key fairness pitfalls enumerated in findings: process isolation, cold-vs-warm compilation (incl. CUDA JIT disk cache), epoch pre-subtraction for master, per-call BLSMemory allocation inside timed region (host arrays are page-aligned NOT pinned — transfers synchronous in both versions), grid/work matching, n=3-median statistics with no dispersion, host-CPU heterogeneity polluting the 7-GPU "vs astropy" column, and the guarded eebls_gpu_batch ndata>10K regression.

confirmed.title: astropy BoxLeastSquares comparison semantics (fairness-critical)
confirmed.detail: API (astropy 7.2.0, pinned in docs): model = BoxLeastSquares(t, y, dy); results = model.power(period, duration, objective='likelihood' (default) or 'snr', method='fast' (default, binned) or 'slow' (exact), oversample=10 (bins per duration)). KEY SEMANTIC DIFFERENCES vs cuvarbase: (1) astropy durations are ABSOLUTE times (days) and the SAME duration array is evaluated at EVERY period — cuvarbase searches fractional q=duration/period between qmin and qmax with a dlogq-spaced ladder and noverlap phase oversampling, optionally per-frequency (Keplerian) q bounds. A fixed astropy duration grid (as in benchmark_algorithms.py) tests wildly different q at P=0.5d vs P=500d; conversely cuvarbase's q-ladder size varies per frequency. (2) astropy power values (likelihood or SNR) are NOT comparable to cuvarbase's SR normalization 1 - chi2/chi2_0 — compare wall time + peak-period recovery (and optionally rank correlation of periodograms), never raw power. (3) astropy's native grid generator autoperiod(duration, minimum_n_transit=3, frequency_factor=1.0) produces a uniform-in-frequency grid; for grid-matched timing pass the identical period array (float64) to astropy that you pass (as 1/freqs, float32) to cuvarbase. (4) Work matching options: (a) headline 'survey task' framing — each code uses its own recommended grid for the same physical search (period range, q/duration coverage), report total trials per code alongside time; (b) strict kernel framing — use cuvarbase eebls_gpu_custom(t,y,dy,freqs,q_values,phi_values) to evaluate exactly astropy's (period,duration,phase) lattice. (5) astropy method='fast' is single-threaded C — record host CPU model and state 1 core; do not let pod-to-pod CPU differences masquerade as GPU differences (the existing by_gpu 'vs astropy' column has this exact problem: each pod's astropy ran on a different host CPU, which partly explains the 257-354x spread).

confirmed.title: transitleastsquares comparison semantics
confirmed.detail: pip package 'transitleastsquares' (Hippke & Heller 2019). API: model = transitleastsquares(t, y, dy); results = model.power(period_min=, period_max=, oversampling_factor=3 (recommended 2-5), duration_grid_step=1.1, use_threads=N, R_star=/M_star= ...). It GENERATES ITS OWN period grid (Ofir 2014 A3 optimal sampling from stellar parameters) — you cannot inject an arbitrary frequency grid, so only period_min/period_max can be matched; report TLS's native grid size next to cuvarbase's. Multi-threaded via multiprocessing (use_threads, default = all cores) — record core count; per-core normalization is informative but the honest headline is wall-time per LC on the stated host. It fits a limb-darkened physical transit template and reports SDE, not BLS SR — it is a DIFFERENT, more sensitive statistic, so frame as 'transit-search wall time at matched period range', not per-frequency throughput, and never compare power values. Note: cuvarbase's own TLS was cut from v1.0 (rework targeted at v1.1); benchmark_algorithms.py still contains a tls bench wired to cvb_tls + transitleastsquares — verify cvb_tls importability before including TLS rows in the campaign, or scope the campaign to BLS/LS only. batman-package (TLS dep for some features) is not installed locally; pods need it.

confirmed.title: Protocol pitfalls checklist for apples-to-apples fairness
confirmed.detail: (1) PROCESS ISOLATION: master and v1.0 in separate venvs/processes (same package name, import-time pycuda context). Use git worktree + per-side venv + subprocess harness. (2) WARM/COLD COMPILATION: v1.0 caches kernels (LRU, _get_cached_kernels), master recompiles per call. Report cold (first call, fresh process) and warm (steady state) separately; for kernel-only comparisons pass functions=compile_bls(...) to both. Control the CUDA JIT disk cache (~/.nv/ComputeCache or CUDA_CACHE_DISABLE=1) for cold runs. LS similarly: reuse LombScargleAsyncProcess (compile ~150ms vs 3-16ms compute) and batched_run_const_nfreq(batch_size=1). (3) TRANSFER/ALLOCATION INCLUSION: with memory=None each eebls_gpu_fast call allocates BLSMemory and does H2D/D2H synchronously (host arrays page-aligned, NOT pinned, both versions) — decide and state whether per-LC allocation+transfer is in the timed region (it is, in all current scripts); for throughput claims also measure memory-reuse mode. (4) GRID MATCHING: same float32 freqs array to both cuvarbase versions; same qmin/qmax/dlogq/noverlap/dphi (defaults already identical); per-frequency Keplerian q bounds via keplerian_freq_grid(return_qvals=True) only exist in v1.0 — for master pass the same arrays via its qmin/qmax array support (master supports array qmin/qmax too). (5) EPOCH: pre-subtract t.min() so master isn't corrupted by float32 BJD. (6) STATISTICS: current n=3 median with no dispersion; rigorous campaign should use >=10 repeats after >=2 warmups, report median+IQR (and min), fixed seeds per config, multiple LC realizations (not 1 seed) for detection metrics, and log nvidia-smi clocks/temp/power during runs to catch thermal throttling; persistence mode where available. (7) TIMING METHOD: standardize on synchronized wall-clock (cuda.Context.synchronize() + perf_counter) for end-to-end numbers; CUDA events only for kernel-level microbenchmarks; never mix in one table (current scripts mix). (8) CPU BASELINE COMPARABILITY: pin astropy (7.2.0; re-run if 8.0 ships with LRA-NUFFT LS), nifty-ls version, record host CPU model/cores per pod; don't compare 'vs astropy' ratios across pods with different CPUs — either run all CPU baselines on one fixed host or report GPU ms/LC as the primary cross-GPU metric. (9) TIMEOUTS: label timeout-derived numbers as lower bounds (existing >27x/>15x convention is correct). (10) KNOWN REGRESSIONS: eebls_gpu_batch is ~12x slower at ndata=20K (UserWarning above 10K) — use single-LC path for TESS/Kepler profiles; batched_run_const_nfreq default is now batch_size=1 (was 10). (11) FLOAT32 vs FLOAT64: cuvarbase is float32, astropy/TLS float64 — validate agreement via peak recovery/correlation (>0.999 convention from FFA work), not rtol on power. (12) COST CLAIMS: pricing table is 2025-Q4/Feb-2026 RunPod community rates — refresh before republishing $/M-LC numbers.
